relationship: creation-judgment background for lifelong toil and return to earth
rationale: Sirach places Adam's children under a burden from birth until return to the mother of all; Genesis assigns Adam painful lifelong labor until he returns to the earth from which he was taken.
source_text: Great occupation was created for every person, and a heavy yoke lies upon Adam’s sons, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day they return to the mother of all:

target_units.text: And to Adam He said: Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree of which alone I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your labours; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life.
Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the plants of the field.
By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for earth you are, and unto earth you shall return.

relationship: parallel lifelong burden of the fear of death
rationale: Sirach names fearful expectation of death within humanity's burden; Hebrews likewise describes lifelong bondage through fear of death, then announces release through Christ.
source_text: their thoughts and fear of heart, anxious expectation, the day of death.

target_units.text: Therefore, since the children have shared in blood and flesh, He Himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death He might render powerless the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil,
and release those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their whole lives.

relationship: related leveling of social ranks before mortality
rationale: Sirach includes both the enthroned and those low in earth and ashes in the human burden; Job places kings, rulers, small and great together in death's rest. The shared mortal condition is viewed from different sides of life and death.
source_text: From the one seated upon a glorious throne to the one brought low in earth and ashes,

target_units.text: Now I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept and rested
with kings, counselors of the earth, who exulted in swords,
or with rulers who had much gold, who filled their houses with silver,
or like a miscarriage coming out of a mother’s womb, or like infants who never saw light.
There the ungodly kindled the fury of anger; there those worn out in body rested.
Together the age-old ones did not hear a tax collector’s voice.
Small and great are there, and the servant does not fear his master.

relationship: parallel trouble persisting despite wealth and status
rationale: Sirach includes those wearing blue and a crown as well as those in raw linen in anger and trouble; Ecclesiastes describes a wealth-holder's days as darkness, mourning, anger and sickness. Wealth supplies no exemption in either account.
source_text: from the one wearing blue and a crown to the one clothed in raw linen, there are anger, jealousy, trouble, upheaval, fear of death, resentment, and strife.

target_units.text: There is a sickness I have seen beneath the sun: wealth kept by its possessor to his harm,
and that wealth will be lost through a grievous distraction, and he fathered a son with nothing in his hand.
As he came naked from his mother’s womb, he will return to depart as he came. He will take nothing from his toil to carry in his hand.
This too is a grievous sickness: just as he came, so he will depart. What surplus has he from toiling for the wind?
All his days are in darkness and mourning, with much anger, sickness and wrath.

relationship: related failure of nighttime to bring relief
rationale: Sirach turns from daytime burdens to sleep that changes awareness, developed as troubled dreams in 40:6; Ecclesiastes says the burdened heart does not sleep at night. Dream disturbance and sleeplessness are distinct forms of unrest.
source_text: Even at the time of rest upon a bed, night’s sleep alters his awareness.

target_units.text: For what comes to a person from all his toil and the resolve of his heart with which he toils beneath the sun?
For all his days are pain, and his distraction is anger; even at night his heart does not sleep. This too is futility.

relationship: close bed-rest disturbed by frightening dreams
rationale: Sirach's sleeper is troubled by a vision of his heart; Job likewise hopes for comfort from his bed but is frightened by dreams and overwhelmed by visions.
source_text: He rests a little, almost nothing; then in sleep, as on a day of keeping watch, he is troubled by his heart’s vision, like someone who escaped from battle.

target_units.text: I said, ‘My bed will comfort me; on my couch I will privately bring up a matter with myself,’
Thou frightenest me with dreams and overwhelmest me with visions.

relationship: related waking discovery of a dream's unreality
rationale: Sirach's dreamer awakens to find there was nothing to fear; Isaiah's dreamers awaken to find their hoped-for refreshment unreal. Both contrast dream experience with waking reality, with opposite emotional outcomes.
source_text: At his time of need he woke, marveling that there was nothing to fear.

target_units.text: Like someone dreaming in sleep will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Ariel, all who marched against Jerusalem, and all assembled against her and afflicting her.

They will be like people drinking and eating in sleep; when they rise, their dream is futile. As a thirsty person dreams of drinking but wakes still thirsty, his soul having hoped in vain, so will be the wealth of all nations who marched against Mount Zion.

relationship: close common mortal condition of humans and beasts
rationale: Sirach extends the preceding burdens to human and beast alike; Ecclesiastes likewise gives humans and beasts one mortal fate. Sirach's sevenfold intensification for sinners is additional.
source_text: This is with all flesh, from human being to beast, and for sinners sevenfold beyond these things:

target_units.text: For the fate of human beings and the fate of the beast is one fate for them: as one dies, so the other dies, and all have one breath. What advantage has a human being over the beast? None, for everything is futility.

relationship: close catalogue of destructive judgments
rationale: Sirach lists death, blood, sword and famine among calamities; Ezekiel likewise joins death and blood with sword and famine in judgments affecting humans and livestock. The catalogues overlap without being identical.
source_text: death, blood, strife, sword, calamities, famine, crushing, and scourge.

target_units.text: Or even if I send death upon that land and pour My wrath upon it in blood, to destroy human and livestock from it,
and Noah, Daniel and Job were within it, as I live, says the Lord, neither sons nor daughters would be left; they would rescue their own lives by their righteousness.
Thus says the Lord: Even if I send My four evil retributions—sword, famine, evil beasts and death—against Jerusalem, to destroy human and livestock from her,

relationship: explicit flood-judgment background
rationale: Sirach connects the flood with the lawless; Genesis describes earth filled with unrighteousness and God's ensuing announcement of a flood that destroys flesh.
source_text: All these things were created against the lawless, and because of them the flood occurred.

target_units.text: And the earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with unrighteousness.
And the Lord God looked upon the earth, and it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth.
And God said to Noah, “The time of all mankind has come before Me, for the earth is filled with unrighteousness because of them; and behold, I am destroying them and the earth.
“Therefore make yourself an ark of squared timber. Make compartments within the ark, and coat it inside and out with pitch.
And this is how you shall make it: the ark shall be three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
Make the ark taper toward the top, and finish it to a cubit above. Set the door of the ark in its side, and make it with lower, second, and third storeys.
“And behold, I am bringing a flood of water upon the earth, to destroy all flesh beneath heaven in which is the breath of life. Everything upon the earth shall die.

relationship: close return to the material of earthly origin
rationale: Sirach says everything from earth returns to earth; Ecclesiastes likewise says all came from dust and all return to dust.
source_text: Everything from earth returns to earth, and what comes from waters returns to the sea.

target_units.text: All go to one place; all came from dust, and all return to dust.

relationship: close waters returning to the sea
rationale: Sirach says what comes from waters returns to the sea; Ecclesiastes likewise describes all streams going to the sea and returning to their course. This addresses the water clause separately from the earth-return clause.
source_text: Everything from earth returns to earth, and what comes from waters returns to the sea.

target_units.text: All the streams go to the sea, yet the sea will not be filled. To the place where the streams go, there they return to go again.

relationship: parallel disappearance of wickedness and lasting righteousness
rationale: Sirach contrasts erased bribery and injustice with enduring faithfulness; Proverbs contrasts the impious disappearing in a storm with the righteous being saved forever. Deeds and their practitioners are expressed differently.
source_text: Every bribe and injustice will be erased, but faithfulness will stand for ever.

target_units.text: When a storm passes by, the impious disappears, but the righteous turns aside and is saved for ever.

relationship: close dwindling of unlawfully acquired wealth
rationale: Sirach says unjust wealth dries up like a river; Proverbs likewise says property pursued with lawlessness becomes less. The thunder and rain imagery belongs to Sirach.
source_text: The wealth of the unjust will dry up like a river and resound like great thunder in rain.

target_units.text: Property pursued eagerly with lawlessness becomes less, but one who gathers for himself with piety will increase; a righteous person has compassion and lends.

relationship: close ungodly offspring as insecure roots and branches
rationale: Sirach denies multiplying branches to ungodly offspring and places unclean roots on rock; Wisdom likewise depicts ungodly descendants as shallow-rooted, insecure growth whose branches are broken off.
source_text: The offspring of the ungodly will not multiply branches, and unclean roots rest upon sheer rock.

target_units.text: But the prolific multitude of the ungodly will be of no use; from illegitimate shoots it will not send a root deep down, nor establish a secure foundation.
For even if it flourishes in branches for a time, standing insecurely, it will be shaken by wind and uprooted by the force of winds.
Unfulfilled branches will be broken off, and their fruit will be useless, unripe for eating, and fit for nothing.

relationship: close enduring significance of generosity to the poor
rationale: Sirach says almsgiving remains forever; the psalm likewise joins giving to the poor with righteousness that remains for an age of an age. Sirach additionally compares kindness to a blessed garden.
source_text: Kindness is like a garden amid blessings, and almsgiving will remain for ever.

target_units.text: He scattered gifts; he gave to the poor. His righteousness remains for an age of an age; his horn will be raised in glory.

relationship: parallel sweetness of enjoying one's labor
rationale: Sirach calls a worker's and self-sufficient person's life sweet; Ecclesiastes likewise calls enjoyment of one's toil and portion good and God's gift. Sirach's higher ranking of finding treasure is not repeated there.
source_text: The life of a self-sufficient person and a worker will be sweet, but above both is the one who finds treasure.

target_units.text: Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and see goodness in all one’s toil beneath the sun during the numbered days of life God has given, for that is one’s portion.
Moreover, every person to whom God has given wealth and possessions, and whom He has empowered to eat from them, take his portion and rejoice in his toil—this is God’s gift.

relationship: related exceptional value of a good wife
rationale: Sirach values a blameless wife above children and city-building as sources of a name; Proverbs likewise values a courageous wife above costly stones and describes her lifelong good toward her husband. The comparison standards differ.
source_text: Children and the building of a city establish a name, but a blameless wife is reckoned above both.

target_units.text: A courageous woman—who will find her? Such a woman is more precious than costly stones.
Her husband’s heart is confident in her; such a woman will not lack fine spoils.
For she works good things for her husband throughout her life.

relationship: parallel preference for wisdom over other prized goods
rationale: Sirach ranks love of wisdom above wine and music that gladden the heart; Proverbs likewise declares wisdom better than precious wealth. It does not repeat the particular wine-and-music comparison.
source_text: Wine and music gladden the heart, but love of wisdom is above both.

target_units.text: Blessed is the person who found wisdom, the mortal who saw good sense,
for trading in her is better than treasures of gold and silver.
She is more valuable than costly stones; nothing evil will stand against her. She is readily known to all who approach her, and nothing precious is worthy of her.

relationship: close sweetness attributed to good speech
rationale: Sirach rates a pleasant tongue above sweet instrumental melodies; Proverbs likewise calls good words sweet honeycombs that heal life, using a food image rather than music.
source_text: Flute and harp sweeten melodies, but a pleasant tongue is above both.

target_units.text: Good words are honeycombs, and their sweetness is healing of the life.

relationship: related distinctive companionship of husband and wife
rationale: Sirach places a wife with her husband above other timely companionship; Genesis describes the corresponding helper and the husband cleaving to his wife as one flesh. It supplies the marital bond, without Sirach's ranking of friends.
source_text: Friend and companion meet at the right time, but above both is a wife with her husband.

target_units.text: And the Lord God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. Let Us make him a helper corresponding to him.”

And God also formed from the earth every wild beast of the field and every bird of heaven, and brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. And whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name.
And Adam gave names to all the cattle, all the birds of heaven, and all the wild beasts of the field. But for Adam no helper like himself was found.
And God cast a deep sleep upon Adam, and he slept. And He took one of his ribs and filled its place with flesh.
And the Lord God fashioned the rib He had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam.
And Adam said: This, at last, is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called Woman, for she was taken from her husband.
For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.

relationship: internal parallel in almsgiving's rescuing power
rationale: Sirach 40:24 ranks almsgiving's rescue above help in affliction; 29:12-13 likewise says stored almsgiving rescues from every affliction and fights more effectively than weapons.
source_text: Brothers and help are for a time of affliction, but almsgiving will rescue beyond both.

target_units.text: Store up almsgiving in your chambers, and it will rescue you from every affliction.
More than a strong shield and more than a weighty spear, it will fight for you against an enemy.

relationship: related preference for wise counsel over precious metals
rationale: Sirach places counsel above the stability supplied by gold and silver; Proverbs prefers discipline and knowledge to silver and gold and makes counsel and security possessions of Wisdom.
source_text: Gold and silver will make the foot firm, but counsel proves better than both.

target_units.text: Take discipline rather than silver, and knowledge above tested gold; choose discernment rather than pure gold.
For wisdom is better than costly stones, and nothing precious is worthy of her.
I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling, and I have called upon knowledge and reflection.
The fear of the Lord hates injustice, insolence and arrogance and the ways of wicked people; and I hate the perverted ways of evil people.
Counsel and security are mine; understanding is mine, and strength is mine.

relationship: close absence of lack for those who fear the Lord
rationale: Sirach says there is no lack in fear of the Lord, ranking it above money and strength; the psalm likewise says those who fear Him have no deficiency while even the rich become poor and hungry.
source_text: Money and strength will lift the heart, but fear of the Lord is above both. There is no lack in the fear of the Lord, and in it there is no need to seek help.

target_units.text: Fear the Lord, His holy ones, for there is no deficiency for those who fear Him.
Rich people became poor and hungry, but those who seek the Lord will not lack any good thing. Diapsalma.

relationship: close protective power of the fear of the Lord
rationale: Sirach describes fear of the Lord as a blessed garden sheltering a person; Proverbs likewise calls fear of the Lord a stronghold for the devout, with a different shelter image.
source_text: The fear of the Lord is like a garden of blessing, and it has sheltered a person beyond all glory.

target_units.text: The fear of the Lord is a stronghold for the devout, but ruin for those who do evil.

relationship: related preference for self-support over dependence
rationale: Sirach urges avoiding a life of begging; Paul likewise urges work with one's hands so as to need no one. Sirach's comparison with death is not part of Paul's instruction.
source_text: Child, do not live a life of begging; it is better to die than to beg.

target_units.text: and to make it your ambition to be quiet, to attend to your own affairs, and to work with your own hands, just as we instructed you,
so that you may walk properly toward those outside and have need of no one.

relationship: close concern with eating one's own bread
rationale: Sirach warns against making another person's table one's livelihood; Paul recalls paying for bread through labor and commands the disorderly who will not work to eat their own bread. Paul's specified unwillingness to work is not supplied as Sirach's explanation of every beggar.
source_text: A man who looks toward another’s table has no livelihood reckoned as life; he will defile his soul with others’ dishes. But a knowledgeable and instructed man will guard himself.

target_units.text: nor did we eat anyone’s bread without payment, but with labor and toil we worked night and day so as not to burden any of you.
This was not because we lack the right, but so that we might give ourselves to you as an example for you to imitate.
For even when we were with you, we gave you this command: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat either.
For we hear that some among you are walking in a disorderly way, not working at all but working at everyone else’s business.
Now such people we command and urge in the Lord Jesus Christ to work quietly and eat their own bread.

relationship: related reversal from sweetness in the mouth to harm in the belly
rationale: Sirach pictures shameless begging as sweet in the mouth but fire in the belly; Zophar pictures evil as sweet in the mouth but an asp's gall in the belly. The bodily reversal is shared, while the acts and harmful images differ.
source_text: Begging will be sweet in a shameless person’s mouth, but fire will burn in his belly.

target_units.text: If evil becomes sweet in his mouth, he will hide it under his tongue;
he will not spare it and will not abandon it, and he will hold it inside his throat.
And he will certainly not be able to help himself; an asp’s gall is in his belly.
Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited up; an angel will drag it from his house.

relationship: related death interrupting comfortable possession
rationale: Sirach calls death's remembrance bitter to someone prospering and able to enjoy food; Jesus's rich man plans rest, eating and gladness from stored goods before his life is demanded. The parable additionally judges his misplaced security.
source_text: O death, how bitter is your remembrance to a person at peace among his possessions, to a man free from distraction and prospering in everything, who still has strength to take food!

target_units.text: And I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Rest, eat, drink, be glad!”’
But God said to him, ‘Fool, this very night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?’

relationship: close death desired as relief from distress
rationale: Sirach calls death's sentence welcome to someone exhausted and unable to endure; Job likewise describes afflicted people longing for death as treasure and rejoicing to obtain its rest.
source_text: O death, how good is your sentence to a person in need and declining in strength, extremely old and distracted about everything, resistant and having lost endurance!

target_units.text: For why has light been given to those in bitterness, and life to souls in pain,
who long for death and do not obtain it, digging for it as for treasures,
and become overjoyed if they obtain it?
Death is rest for a man, for God has shut him in.

relationship: parallel mortality shared across human distinctions
rationale: Sirach answers fear of death by recalling preceding and succeeding generations; Ecclesiastes likewise says one event comes to all and they go to the dead. It does not repeat Sirach's direct exhortation against fear.
source_text: Do not fear death’s sentence; remember those before you and those who come afterward.

target_units.text: There is futility in everything: one event comes to the righteous and the ungodly, to the good and the bad, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who sacrifices and the one who does not sacrifice. As the good person, so the sinner; as the one who swears, so the one who fears an oath.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun: one event comes to everyone. Moreover, the heart of human beings is full of evil, and delirium is in their heart during their lives; afterward they go to the dead.

relationship: related universal death and loss of earthly distinctions
rationale: Sirach calls death the Lord's sentence upon all flesh and denies reproach over lifespan in Hades; Ecclesiastes likewise gives all one event and says the dead no longer share in earthly activities. The particular claim about reproach and length of life remains Sirach's.
source_text: This is the sentence from the Lord upon all flesh. Why do you refuse what pleases the Most High? Whether ten or a hundred or a thousand years, in Hades there is no reproach concerning one’s life.

target_units.text: There is futility in everything: one event comes to the righteous and the ungodly, to the good and the bad, to the clean and the unclean, to the one who sacrifices and the one who does not sacrifice. As the good person, so the sinner; as the one who swears, so the one who fears an oath.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun: one event comes to everyone. Moreover, the heart of human beings is full of evil, and delirium is in their heart during their lives; afterward they go to the dead.
Who shares with all the living? There is hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
For the living will know that they will die, but the dead know nothing; they have no further reward, for their memory is forgotten.
Their love, their hatred and their envy have already perished; they have no further share for ever in anything done under the sun.

relationship: related ungodliness affecting the standing of offspring
rationale: Sirach describes sinners' children as loathsome and associated with ungodly dwellings; Wisdom likewise describes ungodly offspring through insecure growth and their parents' wickedness. It specifies unlawful unions rather than Sirach's whole description.
source_text: The children of sinners become loathsome children, those who associate with the dwellings of the ungodly.

target_units.text: But the prolific multitude of the ungodly will be of no use; from illegitimate shoots it will not send a root deep down, nor establish a secure foundation.
For even if it flourishes in branches for a time, standing insecurely, it will be shaken by wind and uprooted by the force of winds.
Unfulfilled branches will be broken off, and their fruit will be useless, unripe for eating, and fit for nothing.
For children born from unlawful unions are witnesses of wickedness against their parents at their examination.

relationship: related loss of inheritance and name among evil offspring
rationale: Sirach predicts the loss of sinners' children's inheritance and enduring reproach; Isaiah's judgment on Babylon's king likewise excludes his children from inheriting the earth and announces destruction of name and offspring.
source_text: The inheritance of sinners’ children will perish, and reproach will remain continually with their offspring.

target_units.text: Prepare your children to be slaughtered because of your father’s sins, so that they do not rise, inherit the earth and fill the earth with cities.”
“I will rise against them,” says the Lord Sabaoth, “and destroy their name, remnant and offspring”—thus says the Lord—

relationship: close offspring bearing witness against parental wickedness
rationale: Sirach says children blame an ungodly father for their reproach; Wisdom likewise makes children of unlawful unions witnesses of wickedness against their parents. The target specifies unlawful unions; Sirach speaks more generally of an ungodly father.
source_text: Children will blame an ungodly father, because they will be reproached on his account.

target_units.text: For children born from unlawful unions are witnesses of wickedness against their parents at their examination.

relationship: covenant background for woe after abandoning God's law
rationale: Sirach pronounces woe on those abandoning the Most High's law; Deuteronomy likewise announces curses for disobeying the commandments and forsaking the Lord.
source_text: Woe to you, ungodly men, who have abandoned the law of God Most High!

target_units.text: And it shall be, if you do not hearken unto the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all His commandments which I command you this day, that all these curses shall come upon you, and overtake you.
Cursed are you in the city, and cursed are you in the field.
Cursed are your storehouses and your reserves.
Cursed are the offspring of your womb, and the produce of your land, the herds of your cattle, and the flocks of your sheep.
Cursed are you when you go out, and cursed are you when you come in.

The Lord send upon you want, and famine, and wasting, in all that you put your hand unto, whatsoever you do, until He destroys you, and causes you to perish speedily, because of your evil practices, because you have forsaken Me.

relationship: related curse extending across the life of covenant-breakers
rationale: Sirach places the ungodly's birth and death under a curse; Deuteronomy's covenant curses include offspring, coming and going, and destruction. It does not use Sirach's birth-to-death formulation.
source_text: If you are born, you will be born for a curse; if you die, you will be allotted to a curse.

target_units.text: Cursed are the offspring of your womb, and the produce of your land, the herds of your cattle, and the flocks of your sheep.
Cursed are you when you go out, and cursed are you when you come in.

The Lord send upon you want, and famine, and wasting, in all that you put your hand unto, whatsoever you do, until He destroys you, and causes you to perish speedily, because of your evil practices, because you have forsaken Me.

relationship: close return of earth-born humanity to earth
rationale: Sirach says what comes from earth departs into earth; Genesis likewise says the human is earth and returns to earth. Sirach adds its distinct statement about the ungodly's curse and destruction.
source_text: Everything that comes from earth will depart into earth; so the ungodly go from a curse to destruction.

target_units.text: By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for earth you are, and unto earth you shall return.

relationship: close erasure of the ungodly name
rationale: Sirach says sinners' names will be blotted out; Proverbs likewise says the impious person's name is extinguished, contrasting it with the praised memory of the righteous.
source_text: People’s mourning concerns their bodies, but the name of sinners, being no good, will be blotted out.

target_units.text: The memory of righteous people is with praises, but the name of the impious is extinguished.

relationship: close good name valued above gold
rationale: Sirach urges care for a name that lasts longer than great gold treasures; Proverbs likewise calls a good name more desirable than wealth and good favor better than silver and gold.
source_text: Take care of your name, for it will remain with you longer than a thousand great treasures of gold.

target_units.text: A good name is more desirable than much wealth, and good favor is above silver and gold.

relationship: close enduring remembrance of a good life
rationale: Sirach contrasts a life's numbered days with the permanence of a good name; the psalm likewise calls the righteous person an everlasting memorial, without stating the lifespan contrast.
source_text: A good life has a numbered span of days, but a good name will remain for ever.

target_units.text: For he will never be shaken; the righteous person will be an everlasting memorial.

relationship: internal verbal repetition about hidden wisdom and treasure
rationale: Sirach 41:14 repeats the question of 20:30 about the benefit of hidden wisdom and unseen treasure, while adding an address to children about preserving instruction.
source_text: Children, preserve instruction in peace. But hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure—what benefit is there in either?

target_units.text: Hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure—what benefit is there in either?

relationship: internal verbal repetition of the better concealment
rationale: Both sayings prefer the person who hides foolishness to the person who hides wisdom; the comparison and the two concealed objects are the same.
source_text: A person who hides his foolishness is better than a person who hides his wisdom.

target_units.text: Better a person who hides his foolishness than a person who hides his wisdom.

relationship: internal distinction between harmful and proper shame
rationale: Sirach 41:16 rejects indiscriminate shame; 4:20-21 likewise distinguishes shame that brings sin from shame that brings glory and favor.
source_text: Therefore, be ashamed in accordance with my word. For it is not good to preserve every kind of shame, and not everything finds approval with everyone in good faith.

target_units.text: Watch for the right time and guard against evil, and do not be ashamed concerning your soul.
For there is shame that brings sin, and there is shame that is glory and favor.

relationship: related parental authority concerning sexual conduct
rationale: Sirach calls for shame before father and mother over sexual immorality; Proverbs likewise joins keeping parental instruction with protection from a married woman. Sirach's separate warning about lying before rulers is additional.
source_text: Be ashamed before father and mother concerning sexual immorality, and before a leader and ruler concerning a lie;

target_units.text: Son, guard your father’s laws, and do not reject your mother’s ordinances.
Fasten them always upon your soul, and collar them around your neck.
Whenever you walk, take her along and let her be with you; when you sleep, let her guard you, so that when you rise she may converse with you,
because the commandment of law is a lamp and a light, and correction and discipline are life’s way,
to preserve you from a married woman and from an alien tongue’s slander.

relationship: legal setting of offenses brought before judges
rationale: Sirach places an offense before judge and magistrate; Deuteronomy describes disputants coming before judges, who condemn the ungodly and determine punishment. The assembly clause is not repeated there.
source_text: before a judge and magistrate concerning an offense, and before an assembly and people concerning lawlessness;

target_units.text: And if there is a dispute between men, and they come unto judgment, and the judges judge them, and justify the righteous, and condemn the ungodly,
then it shall be, if the ungodly man is worthy of stripes, that you shall seat him before the judges, and they shall scourge him before them, by number according to his ungodliness.

relationship: close prohibitions of theft and injustice toward neighbors
rationale: Sirach calls for shame over injustice toward partners and theft in one's residence; Leviticus likewise forbids stealing, defrauding, wronging and robbing one's neighbor.
source_text: before a partner and friend concerning injustice, and before the place where you reside concerning theft;

target_units.text: You shall not steal. You shall not lie. No one shall defraud his neighbour.
And you shall not swear by My name for an unjust cause, and you shall not profane the name of your God. I am the Lord your God.
You shall not wrong your neighbour, neither shall you rob; and the wages of the hired worker shall in no wise remain with you overnight until morning.

relationship: related rebuke of withheld greetings
rationale: Sirach faults silence toward someone who greets a person; Jesus challenges greeting only one's brothers. Both address withheld social acknowledgment, with different immediate situations.
source_text: of contempt in receiving and giving, and of silence toward those who greet you;

target_units.text: And if you greet only your brothers, what are you doing beyond others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same?

relationship: close warning about the sexual gaze
rationale: Sirach calls for shame at looking at a courtesan; Proverbs likewise warns against being captured through eyes and desire for beauty before speaking of a prostitute. Sirach's separate duty toward relatives is additional.
source_text: of looking at a courtesan, and of turning your face away from a relative;

target_units.text: Do not let desire for beauty overcome you; do not be hunted by your own eyes, nor seized by her eyelids.
For a prostitute’s price is as much as one loaf, but a woman hunts men’s precious lives.

relationship: close danger in looking toward another person's wife
rationale: Sirach includes scrutinizing a married woman in its shame list; Proverbs likewise connects desire and the eyes with the danger of approaching a married woman. The portion-and-gift clause is not repeated there.
source_text: of taking away a portion and a gift, and of scrutinizing a married woman;

target_units.text: Do not let desire for beauty overcome you; do not be hunted by your own eyes, nor seized by her eyelids.
For a prostitute’s price is as much as one loaf, but a woman hunts men’s precious lives.
Will someone bind fire in his bosom without burning his garments?
Or will someone walk on fiery coals without burning his feet?
So is the one who goes in to a married woman: he will not be acquitted, nor will anyone touching her.

relationship: related boundary around sexual access to a household slave
rationale: Sirach warns against meddling with a man's maidservant and standing over her bed; Leviticus addresses intercourse with a household slave reserved for a man. The law supplies a specific case and remedy, not all of Sirach's circumstances.
source_text: of meddling with his maidservant—and do not stand over her bed;

target_units.text: And if anyone lies with a woman with an emission of semen, and she is a household slave reserved for a man but has not been ransomed or given freedom, there shall be an inquiry concerning them. They shall not die, because she has not been freed.
And he shall bring his guilt offering unto the Lord beside the door of the Tent of Testimony, a ram for a guilt offering.
And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering before the Lord for the sin he has committed, and the sin he has committed shall be forgiven him.

relationship: internal parallel against reproach accompanying gifts
rationale: Sirach 41:25 forbids reproach after giving; 18:15-18 likewise rejects adding reproach and hurtful words to gifts and depicts the graceless reproaching giver.
source_text: before friends concerning words of reproach—and after giving, do not reproach;

target_units.text: Child, do not add reproach to good deeds, or the grief of words to any gift.
Will not dew bring relief from scorching heat? So a word is better than a gift.
Behold, is not a word beyond a good gift? Yet both are found with a gracious man.
A fool will reproach gracelessly, and a grudging person’s gift makes eyes waste away.

relationship: contrast in the treatment of concealed matters
rationale: Sirach's shame list includes repeating a report and concealing secret words; Proverbs criticizes the double-tongued revealer of plans but calls concealment characteristic of someone faithful. The differing formulations about concealment are preserved.
source_text: of repeating a report you have heard, and of concealing secret words.

target_units.text: A double-tongued man reveals plans in a council, but one faithful in breath conceals matters.

relationship: internal connection between proper shame and favor
rationale: Sirach 41:27 concludes that the prescribed modesty wins favor; 4:21 likewise identifies a kind of shame that is glory and favor, alongside a harmful kind.
source_text: Then you will be truly modest and find favor before every person.

target_units.text: For there is shame that brings sin, and there is shame that is glory and favor.

relationship: close identification of partiality as sin
rationale: Sirach forbids showing partiality so as to sin; James likewise explicitly calls favoritism sin and transgression of the law.
source_text: Do not be ashamed of these things, and do not show partiality so as to sin:

target_units.text: If, however, you fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well.
But if you show favoritism, you commit sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.

relationship: narrative example of accounting among traveling companions
rationale: Sirach includes accounting with partners and fellow travelers among proper acts; Ezra's traveling custodians deliver the entrusted valuables in Jerusalem by number and weight, with a written record. The inheritance clause is additional.
source_text: of an accounting with a partner and fellow travelers, and of giving an inheritance to companions;

target_units.text: The priests and Levites received the weight of silver, gold and vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem, to the house of our God.
We set out from the river Aoue on the twelfth day of the first month to come to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was upon us, and He rescued us from the hand of an enemy and an adversary along the way.
We came to Jerusalem and stayed there for three days.

On the fourth day we weighed out the silver, gold and vessels in the house of our God into the hand of Merimoth son of Ouria the priest. With him was Eleazar son of Phinees, and with them were the Levites Iozabad son of Iesous and Noadia son of Banaia,
everything by number and by weight, and the entire weight was recorded. At that time,

relationship: close demand for accurate scales and weights
rationale: Sirach approves accuracy in scales and weights; Leviticus likewise prohibits injustice in these measures and requires just scales and weights.
source_text: of accuracy in scales and weights, and of acquiring much or little;

target_units.text: You shall do no injustice in judgment, in measures, weights, or scales.
You shall have just scales, just weights, and a just chous. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

relationship: parallel insistence on disciplining children
rationale: Sirach includes much discipline for children among acts not to be ashamed of; Proverbs likewise commands discipline with a rod and describes it as rescuing the child's life. The source's separate treatment of a household slave is not equated with that child instruction.
source_text: of profit from merchants’ sales, of much discipline for children, and of making an evil household slave’s side bleed.

target_units.text: Do not refrain from disciplining a little child, for if you strike him with a rod, he will certainly not die;
for you will strike him with a rod, but rescue his life from death.

relationship: close accounting by number, weight and written record
rationale: Sirach commands handing over by number and weight and recording giving and receiving in writing; Ezra likewise records the received valuables by number and weight and says the entire weight was written down.
source_text: Whatever you hand over, do so by number and weight; every giving and receiving should be in writing.

target_units.text: On the fourth day we weighed out the silver, gold and vessels in the house of our God into the hand of Merimoth son of Ouria the priest. With him was Eleazar son of Phinees, and with them were the Levites Iozabad son of Iesous and Noadia son of Banaia,
everything by number and by weight, and the entire weight was recorded. At that time,

relationship: parallel discipline distinguishing understanding from folly
rationale: Sirach urges discipline of the senseless as part of becoming instructed; Proverbs likewise connects love of discipline with discernment and hatred of rebuke with foolishness. Sirach's explicit inclusion of an extremely old disputant is additional.
source_text: Do not be ashamed of disciplining the senseless and foolish, or an extremely old man who contends with young people. Then you will be truly instructed and approved before everyone living.

target_units.text: One who loves discipline loves discernment, but one who hates rebukes is foolish.

relationship: internal parallel in a father's concern for a daughter's marriage
rationale: Sirach 42:9 describes paternal anxiety over a daughter's unmarried and married future; 7:24-25 likewise directs care for daughters and treats marriage to an understanding man as a major parental task.
source_text: A daughter is a secret cause of sleeplessness to her father, and anxiety about her drives sleep away: in her youth, lest she pass her prime; when married, lest she be hated;

target_units.text: Do you have daughters? Attend to their bodies, and do not make your face cheerful toward them.
Give a daughter in marriage, and you will have completed a great task; give her to an understanding man.

relationship: related concern about sexual conduct in a father's house
rationale: Sirach names the father's fear of a daughter's defilement and pregnancy at home; Deuteronomy addresses a proven charge of sexual misconduct in the father's house. It gives a legal penalty, not Sirach's full set of anxieties about marriage and barrenness.
source_text: in her virginity, lest she be defiled and become pregnant in her father’s home; while with a husband, lest she transgress; and when married, lest she be barren.

target_units.text: But if this matter is true, and the tokens of the young woman’s virginity are not found,

then they shall bring forth the young woman unto the doors of her father’s house, and the men of her city shall stone her with stones, and she shall die; for she has wrought folly among the sons of Israel, bringing harlotry into her father’s house. And you shall remove the evil one from among yourselves.

relationship: internal verbal parallel about a headstrong daughter
rationale: Both command a firm watch over a headstrong daughter; 42:11 develops the prospect of public shame, while 26:10 speaks of her finding and using freedom.
source_text: Keep a firm watch over a headstrong daughter, lest she make you a delight to enemies, a subject of talk in the city, and an outcast of the people, and put you to shame among a great multitude.

target_units.text: Keep a firm watch over a headstrong daughter, so that she does not find freedom and use it for herself.

relationship: close warning against beauty capturing the eyes
rationale: Sirach forbids gazing at a person's beauty; Proverbs likewise warns against desire for beauty and capture through one's eyes, in a specific sexual warning. Sirach's broader wording and instruction about sitting among women are preserved.
source_text: Do not gaze at any person’s beauty, and do not sit among women.

target_units.text: Do not let desire for beauty overcome you; do not be hunted by your own eyes, nor seized by her eyelids.

relationship: close divine works accomplished by the Lord's word
rationale: Sirach introduces recollection of the Lord's works by saying they are through His words; the psalm likewise says the heavens were established by His word and creation came to be at His command.
source_text: I will now remember the Lord’s works and recount what I have seen. By the Lord’s words are His works.

target_units.text: By the Lord’s word the heavens were established, and by the spirit of His mouth all their power.
He gathers the sea’s waters like a wineskin; He places the deeps in storehouses.
Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all who inhabit the world be shaken before Him.
For He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created.

relationship: parallel sun and heavens displaying divine glory
rationale: Sirach joins the sun's comprehensive shining with the Lord's glory filling His work; the psalm likewise begins with heavens recounting God's glory and describes the sun's heaven-spanning course and heat.
source_text: The shining sun has looked upon everything, and His work is full of the Lord’s glory.

target_units.text: The heavens recount God’s glory, and the firmament announces the work of His hands.
Day pours forth an utterance to day, and night announces knowledge to night.
There are no utterances or words whose voices are not heard.
Their sound went out into all the earth, and their utterances to the limits of the inhabited world. In the sun He set His dwelling.
And he is like a bridegroom coming out of his bridal chamber; he will exult like a giant to run his way.
His going out is from heaven’s edge, and his arrival reaches heaven’s edge; there is no one who will be hidden from his heat.

relationship: close inability to enumerate all divine wonders
rationale: Sirach says even the holy ones cannot recount all the Lord's wonders; the psalm likewise speaks of announcing His wonders and finding them multiplied beyond number.
source_text: He has not enabled the Lord’s holy ones to recount all His wonders, which the Lord Almighty established so that everything might stand firm in His glory.

target_units.text: Many are the wonders Thou hast done, Lord my God, and in Thy purposes there is no one who can be compared with Thee. I announced and spoke; they multiplied beyond number.

relationship: close divine scrutiny of the heart's depth
rationale: Sirach says the Most High traces out the heart and its intricate workings; Jeremiah likewise calls the heart deep beyond all things and identifies the Lord as its examiner. Sirach also speaks of the abyss and universal knowledge.
source_text: He has traced out the abyss and the heart and considered their intricate workings. For the Most High knows all knowledge and has looked upon the sign of the age,

target_units.text: The heart is deep beyond all things, and so is a human; and who will know him?
I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

relationship: close divine announcement of events before they occur
rationale: Sirach attributes announcement of past and future to God; Isaiah likewise identifies God as announcing last things before they came to be and bringing His counsel to fulfillment.
source_text: announcing what has passed and what will be, and uncovering the traces of hidden things.

target_units.text: Remember the former things from eternity, for I am God, and there is none besides Me,
announcing the last things beforehand, before they came to be—and together they were fulfilled. I said, ‘All My counsel will stand, and I will do everything I have planned,’

relationship: close disclosure of hidden things by divine knowledge
rationale: Sirach says God uncovers traces of hidden things; Daniel's blessing likewise says He reveals deep and dark things and knows what is in darkness. This addresses the disclosure clause separately from the announcement of past and future.
source_text: announcing what has passed and what will be, and uncovering the traces of hidden things.

target_units.text: and cried out, “The name of the great Lord will be blessed for ever, because wisdom and majesty belong to Him.
He changes seasons and times, transfers kings and appoints them, gives wisdom to the wise and understanding to those who possess knowledge,
reveals deep and dark things, knows what is in darkness and what is in light, and with Him is a dwelling.

relationship: close divine discernment from which nothing is hidden
rationale: Sirach says no thought or word escapes God; Hebrews likewise describes God's word judging the heart's thoughts and intentions and denies that any creature is hidden before Him. The references to human speech and God's discerning word are distinct.
source_text: No thought has escaped Him; not even one word has been hidden from Him.

target_units.text: For the word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword, penetrating as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
And no created thing is hidden before Him, but all things are naked and laid open to His eyes, to whom we must give account.

relationship: close denial that God needs a counselor
rationale: Sirach says God has needed no counselor; Isaiah likewise asks who became His counselor, instructed Him or showed Him understanding.
source_text: He has set in order the great things of His wisdom, as He exists before the age and into the age. Nothing has been added or diminished, and He has had no need of any counselor.

target_units.text: Who knew the Lord’s mind, and who became His counselor to instruct Him?
With whom did He take counsel, and who instructed Him? Who showed Him judgment, or who showed Him the way of understanding?

relationship: close permanence without addition or subtraction
rationale: Sirach says nothing is added or diminished in the ordering of divine wisdom; Ecclesiastes likewise says God's work endures forever and nothing can be added or taken from it.
source_text: He has set in order the great things of His wisdom, as He exists before the age and into the age. Nothing has been added or diminished, and He has had no need of any counselor.

target_units.text: I knew that everything God has done will endure for ever. Nothing can be added to it, and nothing taken from it; God has done this so that people may fear before Him.

relationship: close enduring creation obeying divine command
rationale: Sirach says the works remain forever and all obey; the psalm likewise describes created things established for the age and earthly elements fulfilling God's word.
source_text: All these live and remain for ever for every need, and all obey.

target_units.text: Let them praise the Lord’s name, for He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created.
He established them for the age and for the age of the age; He set a command, and it will not pass away.
Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps,
fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind—all fulfilling His word,

relationship: internal verbal parallel of paired opposites
rationale: Sirach 42:24 says all things are paired opposite one another; 33:14-15 likewise applies two-by-two opposition to the Most High's works, illustrating it with good and evil, life and death.
source_text: All things are paired, one opposite another, and He has made nothing deficient.

target_units.text: Good stands opposite evil, and life opposite death; so a sinner stands opposite a godly person.
Look in this way at all the Most High’s works: two by two, one opposite the other.

relationship: related satisfaction in beholding divine glory
rationale: Sirach asks who will be filled by beholding God's glory; the psalmist confidently expects satisfaction when that glory appears.
source_text: One has confirmed the good things of another. Who will be filled with beholding His glory?

target_units.text: But I, in righteousness, will appear before Thy face; I will be satisfied when Thy glory appears.

relationship: close firmament displaying divine glory
rationale: Sirach presents the clear firmament and heavenly appearance as a vision of glory; the psalm likewise says the heavens recount God's glory and the firmament announces His handiwork.
source_text: The pride of the heights is the clear firmament, the appearance of heaven in a vision of glory.

target_units.text: The heavens recount God’s glory, and the firmament announces the work of His hands.

relationship: creation background for the sun's appointed work
rationale: Sirach calls the rising sun a wondrous instrument made by the Most High; Genesis likewise describes God making and setting the greater light to rule the day and shine upon earth. The sun's announcement is Sirach's personification.
source_text: The sun, appearing, announces as it rises: a wondrous instrument, a work of the Most High.

target_units.text: And God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; He made the stars also.
And God set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth,
to rule the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good.

relationship: close inescapable heat of the sun
rationale: Sirach asks who can withstand the sun's burning heat; the psalm likewise says no one is hidden from its heat as it crosses heaven.
source_text: At its noon it dries out the land; who will withstand its burning heat?

target_units.text: His going out is from heaven’s edge, and his arrival reaches heaven’s edge; there is no one who will be hidden from his heat.

relationship: parallel heavenly lights made and ordered by divine command
rationale: Sirach praises the Lord who made the sun and directs its course by His words; the psalm likewise summons the sun among the heavenly lights created and established by God's command.
source_text: Great is the Lord who made it, and by His words it hastened on its course.

target_units.text: Praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all the stars and the light.
Praise Him, heavens of heavens, and the water above the heavens.
Let them praise the Lord’s name, for He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created.
He established them for the age and for the age of the age; He set a command, and it will not pass away.

relationship: close moon appointed for seasons
rationale: Sirach describes the moon's appointed timing and display of seasons; the psalm likewise says God made the moon for seasons.
source_text: The moon too is always there at its appointed time, a display of seasons and a sign of the age.

target_units.text: He made the moon for seasons; the sun knew its setting.

relationship: related lunar timing of religious observance
rationale: Sirach connects the moon with the sign of a festival; Numbers places new moons alongside feasts among the occasions for offerings and trumpet remembrance. The moon's diminishing course is additional.
source_text: From the moon comes the sign of a festival, a luminary that diminishes as it completes its course.

target_units.text: And in the days of your gladness, and at your feasts, and at your new moons, you shall blow the trumpets over your whole burnt offerings and over your sacrifices of deliverance; and it shall be a remembrance for you before your God. I am the Lord your God.

relationship: parallel contemplation of the glorious starry heavens
rationale: Sirach calls the stars heaven's shining ornament; the psalm likewise joins praise of divine magnificence above heaven with contemplation of the moon and stars founded by God's fingers.
source_text: The beauty of heaven is the glory of the stars, an ornament shining in the Lord’s heights.

target_units.text: Lord our Lord, how wondrous is Thy name in all the earth, for Thy magnificence was raised above the heavens.
From the mouth of infants and nursing children Thou didst prepare praise, because of Thine enemies, to bring down the enemy and the avenger.
For I will see the heavens, works of Thy fingers, the moon and stars which Thou didst found:

relationship: parallel stars standing under enduring divine command
rationale: Sirach says the stars keep their watches at the Holy One's words; the psalm likewise includes stars among the works created and permanently established under His command. It does not use the watchkeeping image.
source_text: At the Holy One’s words they will stand according to His judgment and will never grow slack in their watches.

target_units.text: Praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all the stars and the light.
Praise Him, heavens of heavens, and the water above the heavens.
Let them praise the Lord’s name, for He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created.
He established them for the age and for the age of the age; He set a command, and it will not pass away.

relationship: creation-and-covenant counterpart to the rainbow
rationale: Sirach bids the observer bless the rainbow's Maker; Genesis likewise presents God setting His bow in the cloud, there as a covenant sign. Sirach emphasizes its beauty rather than rehearsing the covenant.
source_text: Look at the rainbow and bless the One who made it, exceedingly beautiful in its radiance.

target_units.text: And the Lord God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant which I give between Me and you and every living creature with you, for everlasting generations:
I set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.
“And when I gather clouds over the earth, My bow shall appear in the cloud.
And I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of all flesh; and the waters shall never again become a flood to blot out all flesh.
“My bow shall be in the cloud, and I will look upon it and remember the everlasting covenant between Me and every living creature of all flesh upon the earth.”

relationship: close encircling radiance of rainbow and glory
rationale: Sirach calls the rainbow a ring of glory around heaven; Ezekiel compares surrounding brightness to a bow in a rainy cloud and identifies the vision with the likeness of the Lord's glory.
source_text: It encircled heaven with a ring of glory; the hands of the Most High stretched it out.

target_units.text: Like the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the arrangement of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the Lord’s glory. I saw it, and I fall upon my face, and I heard the voice of One speaking.

relationship: close snow brought by divine command
rationale: Sirach says God hastens snow by His command; Elihu likewise describes God commanding snow to come upon earth. Sirach additionally specifies the lightning of judgment.
source_text: By His command He hastened the snow and speeds the lightning of His judgment.

target_units.text: The Strong One will thunder wonders with His voice; for He did great things that we did not know,
commanding snow, ‘Come to be upon the earth,’ and a rainstorm, and a storm of rains of His dominion.

relationship: close storehouse image for heavenly weather
rationale: Sirach's opened storehouses stand between references to snow and hail; the Lord's speech in Job likewise describes stored treasures of snow and hail reserved for a time of battle. Sirach's flying-cloud comparison is additional.
source_text: Therefore the storehouses were opened, and clouds flew out like birds.

target_units.text: Did you come to the treasures of snow, and have you seen the treasures of hail?
It is stored away for you for an hour of enemies, for a day of war and battle.

relationship: close mountains shaken at divine approach
rationale: Sirach says mountains shake at God's appearing; the psalm likewise describes shaken mountain foundations and earth as God bends heaven and descends. Sirach's south wind is an additional detail.
source_text: At His appearing the mountains will be shaken; at His will the south wind will blow.

target_units.text: And the earth was shaken and began to tremble; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken because God was angry with them.
Smoke rose in His anger, and fire from His face set things ablaze; coals were kindled from Him.
And He bent heaven and came down, and gloom was beneath His feet.

relationship: close divine thunder-voice shaking the land
rationale: Sirach attributes earth's rebuke to God's thunder; the psalm likewise joins the God of glory's thunder with His powerful voice shaking the wilderness. The particular winds are not repeated there.
source_text: The sound of His thunder rebuked the earth, as did the north wind’s storm and the whirling of wind.

target_units.text: The Lord’s voice is over the waters; the God of glory thundered; the Lord is over many waters.
The Lord’s voice is in strength; the Lord’s voice is in magnificence.
The voice of the Lord, who crushes cedars; and the Lord will crush Lebanon’s cedars,
and He will grind them fine—Lebanon like the calf— and the beloved like a young one-horned animal.
The voice of the Lord, who cleaves a flame of fire.
The voice of the Lord, who shakes the wilderness; and the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh.

relationship: parallel figurative description of God-given snow
rationale: Sirach compares descending snow to birds and a settling locust; the psalm likewise describes God giving snow through a comparison, to wool. The physical images differ rather than describing the same motion.
source_text: Like birds flying down, He sprinkles snow; like a settling locust is its descent. The eye will marvel at the beauty of its whiteness, and the heart will be astounded by its falling shower.

target_units.text: of Him who gives snow like wool, who sprinkles mist like ashes,

relationship: close frost attributed to divine action
rationale: Sirach says God pours frost upon earth; Elihu likewise says frost is given from the Strong One's breath, alongside His direction of water. Salt and thorn points are Sirach's additional images.
source_text: He pours frost upon the earth like salt, and when frozen it becomes points of thorns.

target_units.text: From the Strong One’s breath frost will be given, and He steers the water however He wishes.

relationship: related ice and the fixed surface of the abyss
rationale: Sirach describes ice settling over gathered water like a breastplate; God's questions in Job likewise concern ice's origin and who fixed the abyss's face. The north wind and armor image belong to Sirach.
source_text: A cold north wind will blow, and ice will freeze upon water. It will settle upon every gathering of water, and the water will put it on like a breastplate.

target_units.text: From whose belly does ice come forth, and who gave birth to frost in heaven,
which descends like flowing water? And who fixed the face of the abyss?

relationship: related healing and renewed growth through dew
rationale: Sirach describes healing mist and gladness-bringing dew; Hosea likewise joins healing with God becoming dew to Israel, which blossoms and spreads branches. Physical weather becomes an image of Israel's restoration there.
source_text: A mist quickly brings healing to everything; dew arriving from the scorching heat will bring gladness.

target_units.text: I will heal their dwellings; I will love them openly, because My anger turned away from them.
I will be like dew to Israel; he will blossom like a lily and put down his roots like Lebanon.
His branches will spread, and he will be like an olive tree laden with fruit; his fragrance will be like Lebanon.

relationship: close divine calming of the deep
rationale: Sirach says God stilled the abyss by His purpose; Job likewise says He calmed the sea by strength. Sirach's planting of islands is additional.
source_text: By His purpose He stilled the abyss and planted islands in it.

target_units.text: By strength He calmed the sea, and by knowledge He wounded the great sea creature.

relationship: close sailors' testimony to danger and divine wonders
rationale: Sirach recounts wonder at sailors' reports of sea danger; the psalm likewise describes sailors seeing divine wonders and facing a terrifying storm, then calls for public praise for their rescue.
source_text: Those who sail the sea recount its danger, and we marvel at what our ears hear.

target_units.text: Those going down into the sea in ships, doing work on many waters,
they saw the Lord’s works and His wonders in the depth.
He spoke, and a storm wind stood, and its waves were raised.
They rise as far as the heavens and descend as far as the deeps; their soul melted in evils.
They were troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.
They cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and He brought them out of their distresses,
and commanded the storm, and it settled into a breeze, and its waves fell silent.
They rejoiced because they became quiet, and He guided them to the harbor of their desire.
Let them acknowledge to the Lord His mercies and His wonders to the sons of men,
let them exalt Him in an assembly of the people and praise Him where the elders sit.

relationship: close sea teeming with creatures and a sea monster
rationale: Sirach names the sea's varied living creatures and sea monsters among wonders; the psalm likewise describes countless small and great creatures and a dragon formed by God in the sea.
source_text: There too are strange things and wondrous works, the variety of every living creature, the creation of sea monsters.

target_units.text: Here is the sea, great and spacious; there are creeping things without number, living creatures small with great.
There ships pass, and this dragon, which Thou didst form to play with it.

relationship: close all things sustained by divine word
rationale: Sirach says all things hold together by God's word; Hebrews likewise attributes upholding all things by the word of His power to the Son through whom God made the ages. The comparison concerns sustenance, not an identification of Sirach's messenger with the Son.
source_text: Because of Him His messenger succeeds, and by His word all things hold together.

target_units.text: but in these last days He spoke to us in a Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, through whom He also made the ages.
He is the radiance of His glory and the imprint of His being, upholding all things by the word of His power. Having made purification of sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,

relationship: related comprehensive conclusion to praise beyond full understanding
rationale: Sirach says speech cannot reach the end and concludes that God is everything; Romans likewise praises unsearchable divine wisdom and concludes that all things are from, through and to Him. The comprehensive praise is shared while the concluding formulations differ.
source_text: We will say much and still never reach the end. The conclusion of our words is this: He is everything.

target_units.text: O depth of God’s wealth and wisdom and knowledge! How unsearchable His judgments and untraceable His ways!
“For who knew the Lord’s mind? Or who became His counselor?
Or who gave to Him first, and it will be repaid to him?”
Because from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. To Him be the glory throughout the ages. Amen.

relationship: close Maker surpassing the beauty and power of His works
rationale: Sirach says God is greater than all His works; Wisdom likewise argues that the Master and Maker is better and more powerful than the beautiful and mighty things He created.
source_text: When glorifying Him, where will we find strength? For He is greater than all His works.

target_units.text: If, delighted by their beauty, they supposed these things to be gods, let them know how much better than these their Master is; for the Originator of beauty created them.
And if they were astonished at their power and activity, let them understand from these how much more powerful the One who fashioned them is.

relationship: close praise of the great and fearsome Creator
rationale: Sirach calls the Lord fearsome, exceedingly great and wondrous in power; the psalm likewise announces His wonders, calls Him great and fearsome, and identifies Him as Maker of the heavens.
source_text: The Lord is fearsome and exceedingly great, and His power is wondrous.

target_units.text: Announce His glory among the nations, His wonders among all the peoples.
For great is the Lord and greatly to be praised; He is fearsome above all gods.
For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens.

relationship: close exaltation beyond the measure of blessing and praise
rationale: Sirach urges the greatest possible glorification while saying God will surpass it; Nehemiah likewise calls for blessing the glorious divine name and exalting it above all blessing and praise.
source_text: As you glorify the Lord, exalt Him as much as you can, for He will surpass even that. As you exalt Him, increase your strength; do not grow weary, for you will never reach the end.

target_units.text: The Levites Jesus and Kadmiel said, “Stand up and bless the Lord your God from everlasting to everlasting. They will bless Thy glorious name and exalt it above all blessing and praise.”

relationship: related limit of human sight and recounting of God
rationale: Sirach asks who has seen God and can recount Him as He is; John likewise says no one has seen God, then identifies the only-begotten God as the One who makes Him known. John's specified revelation supplies a distinct development.
source_text: Who has seen Him and will recount Him? Who will magnify Him as He is?

target_units.text: No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has made Him known.

relationship: close known wonders as only a small part of divine action
rationale: Sirach says the hidden things exceed the few works seen; Job likewise calls the described works only parts of God's way and the heard speech a mere drop, and asks who knows when He will act in the strength of His thunder.
source_text: Many hidden things are greater than these, for we have seen few of His works.

target_units.text: Behold, these are parts of His way, and we will hear a mere drop of speech concerning Him. But the strength of His thunder—who knows when He will act?”

relationship: close wisdom given by God with care for the upright
rationale: Sirach says the Creator gives wisdom to the godly; Proverbs likewise says the Lord gives wisdom and guards those acting rightly and revering Him. The creation-of-all clause is not repeated there.
source_text: For the Lord made all things, and He gave wisdom to the godly.

target_units.text: For the Lord gives wisdom, and from His presence come knowledge and understanding.
He stores up salvation for those acting rightly; He will shield their journey,
to guard the ways of righteous ordinances, and He will protect the way of those who revere Him.

relationship: parallel commemoration of earlier generations' notable lives
rationale: Sirach introduces praise of glorious forefathers; Hebrews likewise recalls judges, kings, prophets and others who received testimony through faith. The catalogues have distinct selections and emphases.
source_text: Let us now praise glorious men, our fathers according to their generations.

target_units.text: And what more shall I say? For time will fail me as I recount Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel and the prophets,
who through faith subdued kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions,
extinguished the power of fire, escaped the edges of the sword, were strengthened from weakness, became mighty in battle, and turned back the armies of foreigners.
Women received their dead through resurrection. But others were tortured, not accepting release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection.
And others experienced mockery and flogging, and also chains and imprisonment.
They were stoned, sawn apart, and died by slaughter with the sword. They went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, and mistreated—
of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth.
And all these, though they received testimony through faith, did not receive the promise,

relationship: historical example of a renowned ruler's understanding
rationale: Sirach includes rulers and men of understanding among the praised ancestors; Israel's recognition of divine discernment in Solomon's judgment supplies a concrete example of wise rulership, not an identification of the entire list with him.
source_text: There were those who ruled in their kingdoms, men renowned for power; those who counseled with their understanding, who made declarations in prophecies;

target_units.text: All Israel heard this judgment the king had given, and they feared the king, for they saw that God’s discernment was within him to carry out justice.

relationship: historical example of learned instruction from sacred writings
rationale: Sirach praises leaders who understand writings and instruct wisely; Esdras is described as a ready scribe in Moses's law who seeks, practices and teaches its ordinances. He illustrates that activity without being named by Sirach here.
source_text: leaders of the people in deliberations and in understanding the people’s writings, wise words being part of their instruction;

target_units.text: this Esdras came up from Babylon. He was a ready scribe in the law of Moses, which the Lord, God of Israel, had given. The king granted him his requests, because the hand of the Lord his God was upon him in everything he sought.
Some of the sons of Israel, the priests and the Levites, together with the singers, gatekeepers and Nathinim, went up to Jerusalem in the seventh year of Arthasastha the king.
They came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, in the seventh year of the king.
On day one of the first month he laid the foundation for the ascent from Babylon; on the first day of the fifth month they came to Jerusalem, because the hand of his God was good upon him.
For Esdras had set it in his heart to seek the law, to do it, and to teach ordinances and judgments in Israel.

relationship: historical example of an ancestor's songs and sayings
rationale: Sirach recalls makers of melodies and written verses; Kings records Solomon's three thousand parables and five thousand songs. The target attests his compositions without specifying their writing process.
source_text: those who sought out musical melodies and related verses in writing;

target_units.text: Solomon spoke three thousand parables, and his songs numbered five thousand.

relationship: historical example of abundance, power and peace
rationale: Sirach includes powerful wealthy men living peacefully; Kings portrays Solomon's ample daily provisions, rule beyond the River and peace on every side. It illustrates the description without identifying all such men as Solomon.
source_text: wealthy men furnished with strength, living peacefully in their dwellings.

target_units.text: The appointed officers thus provided for King Solomon and all the orders for the king’s table, each in his month; they did not depart from an instruction. They brought barley and straw for the horses and chariots to the place where the king would be, each according to his assignment.
These were Solomon’s requirements for one day: thirty kors of fine flour and sixty kors of pounded meal,
ten choice calves, twenty pasture-fed cattle, and a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, and choice birds—fattened provisions.
For he was ruler beyond the River, and he had peace on every side around him.

relationship: internal parallel of honored understanding and public praise
rationale: Sirach 44:7 honors earlier people in their generations; 39:9-10 likewise promises lasting praise and public celebration to the person of understanding, developing a form of remembrance later applied to the ancestors.
source_text: All these were honored in their generations and were a source of boasting in their days.

target_units.text: Many will praise his understanding, and it will not be erased for ever. His memory will not depart, and his name will live for generations of generations.
Nations will recount his wisdom, and the assembly will proclaim his praise.

relationship: close remembered name accompanied by praise
rationale: Sirach says some ancestors left a name so that their praises could be recounted; Proverbs likewise joins the memory of righteous people with praises.
source_text: Some of them left a name, so that their praises might be recounted.

target_units.text: The memory of righteous people is with praises, but the name of the impious is extinguished.

relationship: close absence of remembrance across generations
rationale: Sirach describes people and descendants with no remembrance, as though they had not existed; Ecclesiastes likewise denies remembrance of earlier and later generations among those who follow.
source_text: But there are some of whom there is no remembrance, who perished as though they had never existed, becoming as though they had never been born, and their children after them.

target_units.text: There is no remembrance of the first ones, nor will the last ones who have come to be have remembrance among those who will come at the end.

relationship: close merciful service not forgotten
rationale: Sirach says the merciful ancestors' righteous deeds have not been forgotten; Hebrews likewise says God does not forget the work and love shown in service to the saints.
source_text: Yet these were men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten.

target_units.text: For God is not unjust so as to forget your work and the love you showed toward His name by serving the saints, as you still serve them.

relationship: close righteous conduct leaving children blessed
