rationale: Sirach describes the merciful ancestors' offspring as a good inheritance; Proverbs likewise says a person living blamelessly in righteousness leaves children blessed.
source_text: It will remain with their offspring; their descendants are a good inheritance.

target_units.text: One who lives blamelessly in righteousness will leave his children blessed.

relationship: covenant example of blessing extended to an ancestor's offspring
rationale: Sirach says the ancestors' offspring stood within covenants because of them; God establishes an everlasting covenant with Abraham and his descendants and commands its preservation through their generations.
source_text: Their offspring stood within the covenants, and their children did so because of them.

target_units.text: And I will establish My covenant between Me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be your God and the God of your seed after you.
And I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you live as a stranger, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession; and I will be their God.”
And God said to Abraham, “And you shall keep My covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations.

relationship: parallel conjunction of blessed descendants and enduring righteousness
rationale: Sirach promises lasting offspring and unobliterated glory; the psalm likewise joins a strong seed and blessed upright generation with household glory and righteousness that remains forever. Its permanence clause concerns righteousness.
source_text: Their offspring will remain for ever, and their glory will not be blotted out.

target_units.text: His seed will be powerful in the land; a generation of the upright will be blessed.
Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness remains for an age of an age.

relationship: close peaceful burial of the righteous
rationale: Sirach says the ancestors' bodies were buried in peace; Isaiah likewise says the righteous person's burial will be in peace. The lasting name is an additional Sirach theme.
source_text: Their bodies were buried in peace, and their name lives through generations.

target_units.text: See how the righteous man perished, and no one considers it in his heart. Righteous men are removed, and no one understands. For the righteous man was taken from the presence of injustice.
His burial will be in peace; he has been removed from the midst.

relationship: internal verbal repetition of wisdom recounted and praise proclaimed
rationale: Both passages say peoples or nations recount wisdom and the assembly proclaims praise; the earlier learned person's description becomes language for the honored ancestors.
source_text: Peoples will recount their wisdom, and the assembly proclaims their praise.

target_units.text: Nations will recount his wisdom, and the assembly will proclaim his praise.

relationship: explicit Enoch narrative background
rationale: Both say Enoch pleased God and was taken or transferred away. Sirach's characterization of him as an example of repentance is additional to Genesis's account.
source_text: Enoch pleased the Lord and was taken away, an example of repentance to the generations.

target_units.text: And Enoch pleased God for two hundred years after he begot Methuselah, and begot sons and daughters.
And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years.
And Enoch pleased God, and was not found, for God transferred him.

relationship: explicit Noah narrative background for righteousness
rationale: Sirach calls Noah perfect and righteous; Genesis likewise names him righteous and blameless in his generation and says he pleased God. The later flood and the term exchange are not explained by this single target unit.
source_text: Noah was found perfect and righteous; in a time of wrath he became an exchange. Through him a remnant was left to the earth when the flood came.

target_units.text: These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation; Noah pleased God.

relationship: explicit Noah narrative background for the surviving remnant
rationale: Sirach says a remnant remained through Noah when the flood came; Genesis likewise contrasts the destruction of living flesh with Noah and those with him remaining in the ark.
source_text: Noah was found perfect and righteous; in a time of wrath he became an exchange. Through him a remnant was left to the earth when the flood came.

target_units.text: And all flesh that moved upon the earth died: birds, cattle, wild beasts, every creeping thing that moves upon the earth, and all mankind.
Everything that had the breath of life, everything upon the dry land, died.

And He blotted out every living thing upon the face of the whole earth: mankind, cattle, creeping things, and the birds of heaven. They were blotted out from the earth, and only Noah remained, and those with him in the ark.

relationship: explicit Noahic covenant against another universal flood
rationale: Sirach recalls enduring covenants so that all flesh would not be wiped out by a flood; Genesis establishes the covenant with Noah, his seed and living creatures and promises that floodwaters will not again destroy all flesh.
source_text: Everlasting covenants were established with him, so that all flesh might not be wiped out by a flood.

target_units.text: And God spoke to Noah and to his sons with him, saying,
“Behold, I establish My covenant with you and with your seed after you,
and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the cattle, and all the wild beasts of the earth with you, all that came out of the ark.
“And I will establish My covenant with you: never again shall all flesh perish by the waters of a flood, and never again shall there be a flood of water to destroy the whole earth.”
And the Lord God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant which I give between Me and you and every living creature with you, for everlasting generations:
I set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth.
“And when I gather clouds over the earth, My bow shall appear in the cloud.
And I will remember My covenant between Me and you and every living creature of all flesh; and the waters shall never again become a flood to blot out all flesh.
“My bow shall be in the cloud, and I will look upon it and remember the everlasting covenant between Me and every living creature of all flesh upon the earth.”
And God said to Noah, “This is the sign of the covenant which I have established between Me and all flesh upon the earth.”

relationship: explicit Abrahamic fatherhood of many nations
rationale: Sirach calls Abraham a great father of a multitude of nations; Genesis uses the same many-nations promise in establishing his name and covenant. Sirach adds its comparison of his glory with others.
source_text: Abraham was a great father of a multitude of nations, and no one like him was found in glory.

target_units.text: “As for Me, behold, My covenant is with you, and you shall be a father of a multitude of nations.
And your name shall no longer be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham; for I have made you a father of many nations.
And I will increase you exceedingly, exceedingly, and will make nations of you; and kings shall come from you.

relationship: explicit covenant in Abraham's flesh
rationale: Sirach says Abraham entered God's covenant and established it in his flesh; Genesis commands circumcision and explicitly calls it God's covenant upon the flesh.
source_text: He kept the law of the Most High and entered a covenant with Him. He established a covenant in his flesh, and under testing he was found faithful.

target_units.text: And God said to Abraham, “And you shall keep My covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations.
And this is the covenant that you shall keep, between Me and you, and your seed after you throughout their generations: every male among you shall be circumcised.
And you shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin; and it shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and you.

And every male child among you, eight days old, shall be circumcised throughout your generations, the slave born in your house, and the slave bought with silver from any foreigner who is not of your seed.
The slave born in your house, and the slave bought with silver, shall surely be circumcised; and My covenant shall be upon your flesh as an everlasting covenant.
And the uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day, that soul shall be destroyed from his kindred; for he has broken My covenant.”

relationship: explicit Abrahamic testing and faithful response
rationale: Sirach says Abraham was found faithful under testing; Genesis explicitly introduces God's test and concludes the threatened offering with acknowledgment that Abraham fears God and has not withheld his beloved son.
source_text: He kept the law of the Most High and entered a covenant with Him. He established a covenant in his flesh, and under testing he was found faithful.

target_units.text: And after these things God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham, Abraham.” And he said, “Behold, here am I.”
And He said, “Take your son, your beloved, whom you have loved, Isaac, and go to the high land; and offer him there for a whole burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall tell you.”

And Abraham rose in the morning, and saddled his female donkey, and took with him two servants and Isaac his son. And he split wood for the whole burnt offering, and arose and went, and came to the place of which God had spoken to him.
On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place far off.
And Abraham said to his servants, “Stay here with the female donkey; and I and the lad will go over there, and worship, and return to you.”
And Abraham took the wood of the whole burnt offering, and laid it upon Isaac his son; and he took the fire in his hand, and the knife. And the two went together.
And Isaac spoke to Abraham his father, and said, “Father.” And he said, “What is it, child?” And he said, “Behold the fire and the wood; but where is the sheep for the whole burnt offering?”
And Abraham said, “God will provide for Himself a sheep for the whole burnt offering, child.” And the two went together,

and came to the place of which God had spoken to him. And Abraham built an altar there, and laid the wood upon it, and bound together the feet of Isaac his son, and laid him upon the altar, upon the wood.
And Abraham stretched out his hand to take the knife, to slaughter his son.
And an angel of the Lord called to him out of the heaven, and said to him, “Abraham, Abraham.” And he said, “Behold, here am I.”
And he said, “Do not lay your hand upon the lad or do anything to him; for now I know that you fear God, and have not spared your beloved son for my sake.”

relationship: explicit oath, stars and blessing of nations through Abraham's seed
rationale: Sirach combines the divine oath, multiplied offspring like stars and blessing of nations; Genesis joins these same elements in the oath following Abraham's test. Its additional multiplication image is sand by the sea.
source_text: Therefore He assured him by an oath that nations would be blessed in his offspring, that He would multiply him like the dust of the earth, raise his offspring like the stars, and give them an inheritance from sea to sea and from the River to the end of the earth.

target_units.text: And an angel of the Lord called to Abraham a second time out of the heaven,
saying, “By Myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing, and have not spared your beloved son for My sake,
surely I will bless you, and greatly multiply your seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand upon the shore of the sea; and your seed shall inherit the cities of their adversaries.
And in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have listened to My voice.”

relationship: parallel land promise and innumerable earthly particles
rationale: Sirach recalls multiplied offspring like earth's dust and an inheritance; Genesis likewise promises land and offspring as uncountable as the sand of the earth. The supplied texts use dust and sand respectively.
source_text: Therefore He assured him by an oath that nations would be blessed in his offspring, that He would multiply him like the dust of the earth, raise his offspring like the stars, and give them an inheritance from sea to sea and from the River to the end of the earth.

target_units.text: And God said to Abram, after Lot had separated himself from him, “Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, toward the north, and the south, and the east, and the sea.
For all the land that you see I will give to you and to your seed for ever.
And I will make your seed like the sand of the earth. If anyone can count the sand of the earth, then your seed too shall be counted.
Rise, pass through the length and breadth of the land; for I will give it to you.”

relationship: close sea-to-sea and river-to-world-end territorial formula
rationale: Sirach describes the promised inheritance from sea to sea and from the River to earth's end; the royal psalm uses the same territorial pattern for the king's rule. Abrahamic inheritance and royal dominion remain distinct applications.
source_text: Therefore He assured him by an oath that nations would be blessed in his offspring, that He would multiply him like the dust of the earth, raise his offspring like the stars, and give them an inheritance from sea to sea and from the River to the end of the earth.

target_units.text: And he will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the inhabited world.

relationship: explicit renewal of Abraham's promise for Isaac
rationale: Sirach says the promise was established in Isaac because of Abraham; God likewise promises Isaac the land, multiplied seed and blessing of nations, expressly because Abraham obeyed Him.
source_text: In Isaac He established it in the same way, because of Abraham his father.

target_units.text: “And live as a stranger in this land, and I will be with you and bless you; for to you and to your seed I will give all this land, and I will establish My oath which I swore to Abraham your father.
“And I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven, and give to your seed all this land; and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,
“because Abraham your father obeyed My voice, and kept My charges, My commandments, My ordinances, and My statutes.”

relationship: explicit blessing and inheritance given to Jacob
rationale: Sirach recalls blessing and inheritance resting on Jacob; Genesis likewise describes God blessing Jacob, naming him Israel and giving him and his descendants the land promised to Abraham and Isaac.
source_text: He caused the blessing of all people and the covenant to rest upon Jacob’s head. He acknowledged him with His blessings and gave him an inheritance. He distinguished his portions and divided them among twelve tribes.

target_units.text: And God appeared to Jacob again in Luz, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria; and God blessed him.
And God said to him, “Your name is Jacob; you shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.”
And God said to him, “I am your God. Increase and multiply; nations and assemblies of nations shall be from you, and kings shall come from your loins.
“And the land which I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I have given to you; it shall be yours, and I will give this land to your seed after you.”

relationship: historical counterpart to tribal division of the inheritance
rationale: Sirach recalls the division of portions among tribes; Joshua likewise describes tribal leaders allotting the inheritance and the people dividing the land as commanded. Its account specifies particular tribal arrangements rather than repeating Sirach's number twelve.
source_text: He caused the blessing of all people and the covenant to rest upon Jacob’s head. He acknowledged him with His blessings and gave him an inheritance. He distinguished his portions and divided them among twelve tribes.

target_units.text: These are the sons of Israel who received an inheritance in the land of Canaan. Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders of the ancestral houses of the tribes of the sons of Israel assigned it to them.
They inherited by lots, as the Lord commanded through Joshua for the nine tribes and the half-tribe,
from beyond the Jordan. And he gave the Levites no lot among them.
For the sons of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. No portion in the land was given to the Levites, except cities to live in, their allotted lands for the livestock, and their livestock.
As the Lord had commanded Moses, so the sons of Israel did, and they divided the land.

relationship: explicit public honor of Moses
rationale: Sirach calls Moses favored and beloved among people; Exodus likewise says Moses became very great in the sight of the Egyptians, Pharaoh and his attendants. This particular public recognition is not expanded into a statement about every individual.
source_text: From him He brought forth a man of mercy who found favor in the eyes of all flesh, beloved by God and people: Moses, whose remembrance is among blessings.

target_units.text: The Lord gave His people favour in the Egyptians’ sight, and they lent to them. The man Moses became very great in the sight of the Egyptians, Pharaoh, and all his attendants.

relationship: explicit Moses narrative background for glorification
rationale: Sirach says God made Moses glorious; Exodus describes the glorified appearance of his face after speaking with God. The people afraid there are Aaron and Israel's elders, while Sirach separately mentions enemies' fears.
source_text: He made him like the holy ones in glory and magnified him through the fears of his enemies.

target_units.text: As Moses came down from the mountain with the two tablets in his hands, he did not know that the appearance of the skin of his face had been glorified through speaking with Him.
Aaron and all Israel’s elders saw that the appearance of the skin of Moses’ face had been glorified, and they were afraid to approach him.

relationship: explicit signs ceasing at Moses's words
rationale: Sirach says signs ceased through Moses's words; Exodus recounts Moses crying to the Lord concerning the frogs and the Lord doing as he said, bringing relief from that plague.
source_text: By his words He caused signs to cease; He glorified him before kings. He gave him commandments for His people and showed him something of His glory.

target_units.text: Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh. Moses cried to the Lord concerning the appointed limit for the frogs, as Pharaoh had set it.
The Lord did as Moses said. The frogs died in the houses, farmsteads, and fields.
They gathered them in heaps upon heaps, and the land stank.
When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, his heart became heavy and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.

relationship: explicit commandments entrusted to Moses
rationale: Sirach says God gave Moses commandments for His people; Exodus likewise promises him the written tablets, law and commandments. This addresses the law-giving clause separately from the cessation of signs and the sight of glory.
source_text: By his words He caused signs to cease; He glorified him before kings. He gave him commandments for His people and showed him something of His glory.

target_units.text: And the Lord said to Moses, “Come up to Me into the mountain, and remain there; and I will give you the tablets of stone, the law and the commandments which I have written to give them as law.”

relationship: explicit limited disclosure of divine glory to Moses
rationale: Sirach says Moses was shown something of God's glory; Exodus records his request to see it, God's passing glory, and the limits placed on what he could see.
source_text: By his words He caused signs to cease; He glorified him before kings. He gave him commandments for His people and showed him something of His glory.

target_units.text: Moses said, “Show me Thy glory.”
He said, “I will pass before you in My glory and proclaim My name, Lord, before you. I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and compassion on whom I will have compassion.”
He said, “You cannot see My face, for no man shall see My face and live.”
The Lord said, “Behold, there is a place beside Me; you shall stand upon the rock.
When My glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with My hand until I have passed.
Then I will remove My hand, and you shall see what is behind Me, but My face shall not appear to you.”

relationship: close Moses described as both meek and faithful
rationale: Sirach joins Moses's gentleness and faithfulness with his distinctive selection; Numbers likewise calls him exceptionally meek and faithful in God's house, distinguishing his access to God from ordinary prophetic visions.
source_text: In faithfulness and gentleness He sanctified him; He chose him out of all flesh.

target_units.text: And the man Moses was very meek, beyond all the men upon the earth.
And immediately the Lord said unto Moses, Miriam, and Aaron: Come out, all three of you, to the Tent of Testimony. And the three came out to the Tent of Testimony.
And the Lord came down in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the Tent of Testimony. Aaron and Miriam were called, and both came forward.
And He said unto them: Hear My words: If there is a prophet among you unto the Lord, I will make Myself known unto him in a vision, and I will speak unto him in sleep.
Not so My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house.
I will speak unto him mouth to mouth, in visible appearance, and not through riddles; and he saw the glory of the Lord. And why were you not afraid to speak against My servant Moses?

relationship: explicit Moses entering the darkness where God was
rationale: Sirach says God brought Moses into darkness; Exodus likewise contrasts the people standing far off with Moses entering the thick darkness where God was.
source_text: He let him hear His voice, brought him into the darkness, and gave him commandments face to face, a law of life and knowledge, to teach Jacob the covenant and Israel His judgments.

target_units.text: All the people saw the sound, the flashes, the trumpet’s sound, and the smoking mountain. All the people were afraid and stood far away.
And they said to Moses, “Speak to us yourself, and do not let God speak to us, lest we die.”
And Moses said to them, “Take courage; for God has come to you to test you, that His fear may be in you, so that you do not sin.”
The people stood far away, while Moses entered the thick darkness where God was.

relationship: explicit face-to-face speech with Moses
rationale: Sirach recalls divine speech and commandments face to face; Exodus explicitly says the Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as to a friend. That verse does not narrate the entire law-giving.
source_text: He let him hear His voice, brought him into the darkness, and gave him commandments face to face, a law of life and knowledge, to teach Jacob the covenant and Israel His judgments.

target_units.text: The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Then Moses returned to the camp, but his young attendant Joshua son of Nun did not leave the tent.

relationship: close Mosaic instruction described as life
rationale: Sirach calls Moses's instruction a law of life for Israel; Moses likewise commands Israel to preserve and teach the words of the law and says this word is their life.
source_text: He let him hear His voice, brought him into the darkness, and gave him commandments face to face, a law of life and knowledge, to teach Jacob the covenant and Israel His judgments.

target_units.text: And Moses wrote this song in that day, and taught it unto the sons of Israel. And Moses came in and spoke all the words of this law in the hearing of the people, he and Joshua the son of Nun.
And Moses finished speaking unto all Israel,
and said unto them, Give heed in your heart unto all these words which I testify unto you this day, which you shall command your sons to keep and to do, even all the words of this law.
For this is no empty word unto you; for this is your life, and by this word you shall prolong your days upon the land into which you are crossing the Jordan to inherit it.

relationship: explicit selection of Aaron, Moses's brother, for priesthood
rationale: Sirach says God exalted Moses's holy brother Aaron; Exodus commands bringing Aaron the brother and his sons forward to serve as priests. The tribe of Levi is an additional identification in Sirach, also confirmed in the separately read Numbers 18:1-2.
source_text: He exalted Aaron, a holy man like him, his brother from the tribe of Levi.

target_units.text: “And bring to yourself Aaron your brother and his sons from among the sons of Israel, to serve Me as priests: Aaron, and Nadab, and Abihu, and Eleazar, and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron.

relationship: explicit enduring priesthood of Aaron and his sons
rationale: Sirach describes an everlasting covenant granting Aaron priesthood; Exodus likewise gives Aaron and his sons priesthood forever and orders their consecration.
source_text: He established him as an everlasting covenant and gave him the priesthood of the people. He blessed him with beautiful attire and girded him with a robe of glory.

target_units.text: Bring his sons and clothe them with tunics.
Gird them with sashes and put turbans on them. The priesthood shall be theirs for Me for ever. You shall consecrate Aaron’s hands and the hands of his sons.

relationship: close holy priestly attire for honor and glory
rationale: Sirach says Aaron was blessed with beautiful attire and a robe of glory; Exodus likewise orders his holy robe for honor and glory and lists the priestly garments.
source_text: He established him as an everlasting covenant and gave him the priesthood of the people. He blessed him with beautiful attire and girded him with a robe of glory.

target_units.text: You shall make a holy robe for Aaron your brother, for honour and glory.
Speak to everyone skilled in understanding whom I have filled with a spirit of perception. They shall make Aaron’s holy robe for the sanctuary, in which he shall serve Me as priest.

These are the robes they shall make: a breastpiece, a shoulder-piece, a full-length robe, a tasselled tunic, a turban, and a sash. They shall make holy robes for Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests.

relationship: explicit full-length robe and shoulder-piece
rationale: Sirach's list of Aaron's splendid garments includes a full-length robe and shoulder-piece; Exodus lists those garments and their crafted materials. The breeches are addressed in a separate target.
source_text: He clothed him with the fullness of splendor and equipped him with mighty garments: breeches, a robe reaching to the feet, and a shoulder piece.

target_units.text: These are the robes they shall make: a breastpiece, a shoulder-piece, a full-length robe, a tasselled tunic, a turban, and a sash. They shall make holy robes for Aaron and his sons to serve Me as priests.
They shall take gold, blue, purple, scarlet yarn, and fine linen.
They shall make the shoulder-piece of spun fine linen, the work of a skilled weaving embroiderer.

relationship: explicit priestly linen undergarments
rationale: Sirach includes breeches among Aaron's garments; Exodus prescribes linen undergarments for Aaron and his sons to cover the flesh from waist to thighs during sanctuary service.
source_text: He clothed him with the fullness of splendor and equipped him with mighty garments: breeches, a robe reaching to the feet, and a shoulder piece.

target_units.text: You shall make linen undergarments for them to cover the nakedness of their flesh, reaching from the waist to the thighs.

And Aaron and his sons shall wear them when they enter into the Tent of Testimony, or draw near to minister at the altar of the sanctuary; and they shall not bring sin upon themselves, lest they die. It shall be an everlasting statute for him and for his seed after him.”

relationship: explicit pomegranate-and-bell hem with audible sanctuary service
rationale: Both describe pomegranates and bells around the robe and their sound in the sanctuary. Sirach specifies golden bells; the supplied Exodus wording explicitly mentions gold pomegranates and bells between them.
source_text: He surrounded him with little pomegranates, with many golden bells all around, to sound with his footsteps and make an audible ringing in the sanctuary as a remembrance for the sons of His people;

target_units.text: Around the under-robe’s lower hem you shall make little pomegranates like those of a flowering pomegranate tree, of blue, purple, spun scarlet yarn, and spun fine linen; likewise gold pomegranates, with bells between them all around.
Beside a gold pomegranate there shall be a bell and a floral ornament around the under-robe’s hem.
And Aaron’s sound shall be heard when he ministers, as he enters into the sanctuary before the Lord and as he goes out, so that he does not die.

relationship: explicit embroidered oracle-piece of judgment
rationale: Sirach's oracle-piece and colored precious fabric correspond to Exodus's embroidered oracle-piece of judgments, made with gold, blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen.
source_text: with a holy robe of gold, blue, and purple, the work of an embroiderer; with an oracle-piece of judgment, tokens of truth, twisted scarlet, a craftsman’s work;

target_units.text: You shall make an oracle-piece of judgments, embroidered work, according to the pattern of the shoulder-piece, of gold, blue, purple, spun scarlet yarn, and spun fine linen.
It shall be square and doubled, a span long and a span wide.

relationship: explicit truth associated with the oracle-piece
rationale: Sirach includes tokens of truth with the oracle-piece of judgment; Exodus explicitly places Manifestation and Truth upon that oracle-piece, borne by Aaron before the Lord.
source_text: with a holy robe of gold, blue, and purple, the work of an embroiderer; with an oracle-piece of judgment, tokens of truth, twisted scarlet, a craftsman’s work;

target_units.text: And you shall set Manifestation and Truth upon the oracle-piece of judgment; and it shall be upon Aaron’s breast when he enters into the sanctuary before the Lord. And Aaron shall bear the judgments of the sons of Israel upon his breast before the Lord continually.

relationship: explicit engraved tribal stones in gold as a memorial
rationale: Sirach's precious stones, seal-like engravings, gold settings and tribal remembrance correspond to Exodus's twelve named tribal stones and Aaron bearing the names as a memorial. The target follows the actual native units, including the numbering gap before 28:29.
source_text: with costly stones bearing engraved seals in settings of gold, a stoneworker’s work, as a remembrance in carved writing according to the number of Israel’s tribes;

target_units.text: You shall weave into it a fabric set with four rows of stones. The first row shall be a sardius, topaz, and emerald;
the second row a carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper;
the third row a ligure, agate, and amethyst;
the fourth row a chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. They shall be enclosed in gold and bound in gold according to their rows.
The stones shall bear the names of the sons of Israel, twelve according to their names, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes.
You shall make braided chains of pure gold for the oracle-piece.
And Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel upon the oracle-piece of judgment, upon his breast, when he enters into the sanctuary, as a memorial before God.

relationship: explicit gold head ornament with a holy seal inscription
rationale: Sirach recalls a gold crown upon the turban and a seal of holiness; Exodus prescribes a gold plate stamped like a seal with The Lord's consecrated thing and fastened to the headband. Crown and plate are the respective descriptions.
source_text: with a golden crown upon the turban, the impression of a seal of holiness, an honor to boast of, a mighty work, beautifully adorned things desired by the eyes.

target_units.text: You shall make a plate of pure gold and stamp on it like a seal: ‘The Lord’s consecrated thing.’
You shall fasten it to spun blue material so that it may rest on the headband, at the front of the headband.

It shall be on Aaron’s forehead, and Aaron shall remove the sins of the holy things the sons of Israel consecrate, of every holy gift. It shall be on Aaron’s forehead continually, acceptable for them before the Lord.

relationship: explicit Aaronic succession in the holy garments
rationale: Sirach reserves the garments to Aaron's sons and descendants; Exodus likewise gives Aaron's holy robe to his sons and to the priest succeeding him from among them. It does not repeat Sirach's retrospective claim that no outsider ever wore them.
source_text: Before him there had never been such beautiful things. No outsider has ever worn them, but only his sons and his descendants continually.

target_units.text: Aaron’s holy robe shall belong to his sons after him, to be anointed in the garments and have their hands consecrated.
The priest who succeeds him from among his sons shall wear them for seven days; he shall enter the Tent of Testimony to minister in the holy places.

relationship: explicit twice-daily continual offering
rationale: Sirach describes sacrifices wholly offered twice each day continually; Exodus prescribes two lambs each day, morning and evening, as a continual offering through the generations.
source_text: His sacrifices will be wholly offered twice every day, continually.

target_units.text: This is what you shall offer on the altar: two year-old lambs without blemish each day continually, a continual offering.
Offer one lamb in the morning and the second in the evening.
With one lamb offer a tenth measure of fine flour mixed with a quarter hin of beaten oil, and a quarter hin of wine as a libation.
Offer the second lamb in the evening, with the same sacrifice and libation as in the morning, as a fragrant aroma, an offering to the Lord,
as a continual sacrifice throughout your generations, at the doors of the Tent of Testimony before the Lord, where I will be made known to you, to speak to you.

relationship: explicit anointing and consecration of priestly hands
rationale: Sirach recalls oil anointing, filled hands and enduring priesthood; Exodus commands oil poured on Aaron's head, consecration of his and his sons' hands, and priesthood forever.
source_text: Moses filled his hands and anointed him with holy oil. It became an everlasting covenant for him and his offspring, throughout the days of heaven, to minister to Him, serve as priests, and bless His people in the Name.

target_units.text: Take the anointing oil, pour it on his head, and anoint him.
Bring his sons and clothe them with tunics.
Gird them with sashes and put turbans on them. The priesthood shall be theirs for Me for ever. You shall consecrate Aaron’s hands and the hands of his sons.

relationship: explicit Aaronic blessing with the divine Name
rationale: Sirach includes blessing God's people in the Name among Aaron's duties; Numbers commands Moses to instruct Aaron and his sons in blessing Israel and placing God's name upon them. The name clause is within native 6:23.
source_text: Moses filled his hands and anointed him with holy oil. It became an everlasting covenant for him and his offspring, throughout the days of heaven, to minister to Him, serve as priests, and bless His people in the Name.

target_units.text: And the Lord spoke unto Moses, saying:
Speak unto Aaron and unto his sons, saying: Thus you shall bless the sons of Israel, saying unto them (and they shall put My name upon the sons of Israel, and I, the Lord, will bless them):
The Lord bless you and keep you;
the Lord make His face shine upon you, and have mercy upon you;
the Lord lift up His face upon you, and give you peace.

relationship: explicit Aaronic incense making atonement for the people
rationale: Sirach describes Aaron's incense and atoning ministry; Numbers narrates Aaron carrying incense into the outbreak, making atonement and standing between dead and living as the outbreak subsides.
source_text: He chose him from every living person to present an offering to the Lord, incense and a pleasing fragrance as a remembrance, to make atonement for your people.

target_units.text: And Moses said unto Aaron: Take the fire pan, put fire from the altar on it, and place incense on it. Carry it quickly into the camp and make atonement for them, for wrath has gone out from before the Lord; it has begun to strike the people.
And Aaron took it just as Moses had told him and ran into the congregation. The outbreak had already begun among the people. He placed the incense and made atonement for the people,
and stood between the dead and the living, and the outbreak subsided.

relationship: close Levitical teaching of Jacob's ordinances and Israel's law
rationale: Sirach describes Aaron teaching Jacob testimonies and enlightening Israel through law; Moses's blessing of Levi likewise commissions declaration of ordinances to Jacob and law to Israel, alongside incense ministry.
source_text: In His commandments He gave him authority concerning covenants of judgments, to teach Jacob the testimonies and enlighten Israel through His law.

target_units.text: And unto Levi he said, Give unto Levi his manifestations, and his truth unto the holy man, whom they tested in a trial, and reviled at the water of dispute;
who says unto his father and his mother, I have not seen you; and he did not acknowledge his brethren, and disowned his sons. He kept Thine oracles, and preserved Thy covenant.
They shall declare Thine ordinances unto Jacob, and Thy law unto Israel; they shall lay incense in Thy wrath, continually upon Thine altar.

relationship: explicit named rebellion against Moses and Aaron
rationale: Sirach names Dathan, Abiram and Korah's assembly as opponents; Numbers likewise names those men and describes their congregation banding together against Moses and Aaron.
source_text: Outsiders banded together against him and envied him in the wilderness: the men around Dathan and Abiram, and Korah’s assembly in anger and wrath.

target_units.text: And Korah son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, spoke, with Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On son of Peleth, son of Reuben.
And they rose up before Moses, with two hundred fifty men of the sons of Israel, leaders of the congregation, members summoned to the council, men of renown.
They banded together against Moses and Aaron and said: Enough for you! The whole congregation, all of them, is holy, and the Lord is among them. Why do you rise up against the Lord’s congregation?

relationship: poetic retelling of opposition to the Lord's holy Aaron
rationale: Sirach calls Aaron holy and names Dathan and Abiram among the rebels; the psalm likewise calls Aaron the Lord's holy one and names Dathan and Abiram in the ensuing judgment. Its stated action is angering Moses and Aaron; Sirach specifies envy.
source_text: Outsiders banded together against him and envied him in the wilderness: the men around Dathan and Abiram, and Korah’s assembly in anger and wrath.

target_units.text: They angered Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the Lord’s holy one.
The earth was opened and swallowed Dathan and covered Abiram’s assembly.
Fire was kindled in their assembly; a flame burned up sinners.

relationship: explicit divine fire consuming rebellious incense-offerers
rationale: Sirach recalls rebels consumed by divine fire; Numbers identifies the two hundred fifty incense-offerers consumed by fire from the Lord. The earlier context separately narrates the earth swallowing the other rebels.
source_text: The Lord saw and was not pleased, and they were brought to their end in furious wrath. He worked portents upon them, consuming them in His flaming fire.

target_units.text: And fire went out from the Lord and consumed the two hundred fifty men presenting the incense.

relationship: explicit firstfruits allotted to Aaron as an honorable share
rationale: Sirach says Aaron received added glory, an inheritance and first produce for food; Numbers likewise grants him a share of honor from holy gifts and specifies firstfruits of oil, wine, grain and the land's produce.
source_text: He added glory to Aaron and gave him an inheritance. He allotted him the firstfruits of the first produce; He prepared bread in abundance first for them.

target_units.text: And the Lord spoke unto Aaron: And I, behold, have given you charge of the firstfruits; from all things sanctified unto Me by the sons of Israel, I have given them unto you for a share of honour, and unto your sons after you, an everlasting ordinance.

And this shall be yours from the consecrated holy offerings: from all their gifts, and from all their sacrifices, and from every guilt offering of theirs, and from all their sin offerings which they render unto Me; from all the holy things it shall be yours and your sons’.
You shall eat them in the most holy place; every male shall eat them, you and your sons; they shall be holy unto you.

And this shall be yours, the firstfruits of their gifts: from all the presentations of the sons of Israel, I have given them unto you, and unto your sons and unto your daughters with you, an everlasting ordinance. Everyone clean in your house shall eat them.
Every firstfruit of oil, and every firstfruit of wine and grain, their firstfruits which they give unto the Lord, I have given them unto you.
All the first produce in their land, which they bring unto the Lord, shall be yours; everyone clean in your house shall eat it.

relationship: explicit holy offerings eaten by Aaron and his sons
rationale: Sirach says Aaron and his offspring eat the Lord's sacrifices; Numbers likewise gives them the holy offerings and explicitly directs Aaron and his sons to eat them.
source_text: For they will eat the Lord’s sacrifices, which He gave both to him and to his offspring.

target_units.text: And this shall be yours from the consecrated holy offerings: from all their gifts, and from all their sacrifices, and from every guilt offering of theirs, and from all their sin offerings which they render unto Me; from all the holy things it shall be yours and your sons’.
You shall eat them in the most holy place; every male shall eat them, you and your sons; they shall be holy unto you.

relationship: close Lord-as-inheritance formula for Aaron
rationale: Both deny Aaron a landed portion among Israel and identify the Lord Himself as his portion and inheritance.
source_text: But he will inherit nothing in the people’s land, and he has no portion among the people, for He Himself is your portion and inheritance.

target_units.text: And the Lord spoke unto Aaron: You shall not inherit in their land, neither shall you have a portion among them; for I am your portion and your inheritance among the sons of Israel.

relationship: explicit Phinehas's zeal and atonement
rationale: Sirach praises Phinehas's zeal and atonement for Israel; Numbers likewise names Phinehas son of Eleazar, credits his zeal with turning away wrath and says he made atonement for Israel.
source_text: Phinehas son of Eleazar was third in glory, because he was zealous in the fear of the Lord and stood firm when the people turned away, with the goodness of his soul’s eagerness. He made atonement for Israel.

target_units.text: And the Lord spoke unto Moses, saying:
Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has stopped My wrath against the sons of Israel by being zealous with My zeal among them, and I did not consume the sons of Israel in My zeal.
Therefore say: Behold, I give him a covenant of peace.
And it shall be for him and his seed after him an everlasting covenant of priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and made atonement for the sons of Israel.

relationship: poetic counterpart to Phinehas standing and making atonement
rationale: Sirach says Phinehas stood firm amid the people's turning away and made atonement; the psalm likewise describes Baal-peor worship, Phinehas standing and making atonement, and the outbreak ceasing.
source_text: Phinehas son of Eleazar was third in glory, because he was zealous in the fear of the Lord and stood firm when the people turned away, with the goodness of his soul’s eagerness. He made atonement for Israel.

target_units.text: They were initiated to Baal-peor and ate sacrifices of the dead.
They provoked Him with their practices, and the falling multiplied among them.
Phinehas stood and made atonement, and the breaking ceased.
It was reckoned to him as righteousness, from generation to generation for ever.

relationship: explicit covenant of peace and lasting priesthood for Phinehas
rationale: Both join God's covenant of peace for Phinehas with enduring priesthood for him and his descendants.
source_text: Therefore a covenant of peace was established for him, to preside over holy things and His people, so that the majesty of the priesthood might belong to him and his offspring for ever.

target_units.text: Therefore say: Behold, I give him a covenant of peace.
And it shall be for him and his seed after him an everlasting covenant of priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and made atonement for the sons of Israel.

relationship: explicit Davidic covenant and dynastic succession
rationale: Sirach recalls the covenant for David and royal inheritance through sons; the psalm likewise joins the covenant and oath to David with enduring seed and a throne through generations. Sirach adds the comparison with Aaron's inheritance.
source_text: There was also a covenant for David son of Jesse, of the tribe of Judah: the inheritance of a king passes from son to son alone; Aaron’s inheritance belongs also to his offspring.

target_units.text: “I made a covenant with My chosen ones; I swore to David My servant:
‘I will prepare your seed for ever and build your throne from generation to generation.’” Diapsalma.

relationship: close prayer for a wise heart to judge God's people rightly
rationale: Sirach asks for heart-wisdom to judge God's people in righteousness; Solomon likewise requests a heart to hear and judge the people in righteousness, and receives a discerning and wise heart. The royal request provides the parallel to Sirach's concluding wish.
source_text: May He give you wisdom in your heart to judge His people in righteousness, so that their good things may not disappear, and their glory may last through their generations.

target_units.text: Give Thy servant a heart to hear and to judge Thy people in righteousness, discerning between good and evil; for who can judge this weighty people of Thine?”
It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.
The Lord said to him, “Because you have asked this of Me and have not asked for many days for yourself, or wealth, or the lives of your enemies, but have asked for understanding to hear judgment,
behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a discerning and wise heart, so that no one like you has been before you, and no one like you shall arise after you.
